To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

a premature stop codon within the II-3 loop of the DHPR pore subunit (a1S) can be overcome by a restart of translation, and that this restart is not necessarily detrimental to function, as long as a complementary protein fragment can be expressed.

a) a premature stop codon may be bypassed by an unexpected restart at the next in-frame methionine; b) protein-protein complementarity between hemi-C Ca2+ channel proteins can restore DHPR-Ry1 coupling; and c) the DHPR voltage-sensing function can be achieved by a hemi-Ca channel protein that is not an intact II-3 loop.

a premature stop codon within the II-3 loop of α1S can be bypassed by a mechanism involving restart of translation within this loop, and that the two complementary hemi-α1S fragments are capable of protein-protein complementaion and restoring skeletal-type EC coupling.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the molecular mechanism of EC coupling in skeletal muscle and the functional analysis of a frame shift mutant of the dihydropridine receptor pore subunit, which expresses two complementary hemi-DHPR fragments.
the functional consequences of a frame-shift mutation of the DHPR pore subunit (alpha1S) in dysgenic muscle.
the functional analysis of a single-base frame shift mutation in the α1S gene of the dihydropridine receptor (DHPR).
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the DHPR pore subunit is not required for skeletal muscle EC coupling.

a single-base frame shift in the DHPR pore subunit (M1) can be rescued by expression of the complementary protein fragments, and the resulting functional channel can couple the DHPR voltage sensors to the RyR1 channel.
the II-III domain of α1S is not essential for EC coupling.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the frame-shift mutant α1S is a useful genetic tool for the functional analysis of the DHPR pore and the EC coupling mechanism.
the II-III domain of the DHPR pore subunit is not essential for EC coupling.
protein complementation between the N- and C-terminal fragments of α1S can rescue EC coupling, and that the II-III loops are not essential for DHPR-Ryr1 interactions.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a frame-shift mutation in α1S can be used as a tool to study EC coupling.
protein-protein complementarity is an important feature of the DHPR pore subunit that may be used to restore function in cases of premature stop codons.
a premature stop codon does not always lead to a loss of function.
